docs.text: 1 National Tsing Hua University Institute of Technology Management Organizational Behavior Fall 2025 Class meets: Wednesday 9am to 11:50am in Room 120, TSMC Building Instructor: Dr. Yu-Wen Liu Language: Chinese Office: Room 851 TSMC Building Office hours: By appointment Contact: ywliu@mx.nthu.edu.tw COURSE OBJECTIVE: After completing the class, you should become familiar with the major concepts of organizational behavior and issues that managers encounter, and with principles, practices and models that help managers deal with these issues. In addition, you should be able to see how the relationships among people within an organization and relationships among organizations influence organizational effectiveness. DETAILS: Each class will include discussion of readings, recent news and cases. Your grade will be based on your performance in the following three categories. I. Classroom Participation (25%) In-class Discussion The learning experience in a course like this one depends heavily on each student being prepared to actively participate in every class session. Positive participation includes attendance, active involvement in all in-class exercises and discussions, and maintenance of a classroom demeanor that encourages the participation of others. You will be evaluated on the quantity as well as the quality of your contribution and insights. Quality comments possess one or more of the following attributes: (a) Contribute to moving the discussion forward; (b) Offer a different, unique and relevant perspective on the issue; (c) Build on other comments of others; and (d) Include some evidence or analysis of inherent tradeoffs, i.e., demonstrate reflective thinking. Individual weekly personal learning note In addition, closing to the end of every class, each student is required to summarize what you have learned in our class on that day in one page. The one-page summary should include both key ideas from each article and your main takeaway from our class discussion. II. Group Assignments (50%) Weekly group presentation for the selected article/book chapter (15% x 2 = 30%) Every week, two groups of students will be responsible for presenting the key ideas from one selected article or textbook chapter and raising some questions for discussion 2 for that week. The presentation should be done within 20 minutes. Additionally, each group needs to provide at least one additional reading on the selected topic which is published after 2015. These readings can be newspaper, magazine, or journal articles. These additional readings can be written in Chinese or English. Choose one reading from the provided additional readings and develop a 10-minute presentation or activity for the chosen reading. We will leave 20 minutes for discussing questions. Final group project (20%) Each group needs to select one company/business field/industry, identify the challenges the company/business field/industry currently faces through analyzing secondary data, interviewing or observing onsite, and come up with potential solutions to fix the problems that the company/business field/industry are facing. On Oct 29, 2025, each group will hand in their target company/business field/industry and their problems for the term project. All groups need to hand in and present your progress report of the final project on Nov. 26, 2025. The final presentation will be held on Dec 10 & 17, 2025. The content of presentation includes the components below: One company/business field/industry, the challenges, potential solutions, business ideas, and your intended goal. The more details, the better. Final group project delivery Before your group presentation, the ppt file should be sent to the following address ywliu@mx.nthu.edu.tw before 5 pm on Sunday. Please Note that, the final grade on group related assignments might not be the same for all members on a team if someone does not contribute equally to the team projects. Please note that the credit for each team member in the same team might be different if most of your teammates are not satisfied with your contribution. Team Member Assessments: Every team member will • Develop a substantive assessment (min 30 words each) on each team member’s contributions. • Assign a % in 5% increments (e.g. 80%, 95%, 100%, 110%, etc) to each of the other team members, insuring that the total of your percentages adds up to the number of other team members x 100% (so 3 other team members = 300%, 4 other team members = 400%, etc) • Post his/her Team Member Assessments to Assignment. III. Taiwanese Enterprises in Global Markets: A Learning Journey (25%) This project : “世界”，我來了: 跟著台商的腳步走 is to explore the challenges of global expansion from a Taiwanese perspective by learning from Taiwanese enterprises abroad and expatriates. Further instructions will be provided in class. OTHER POLICIES OR NOTES: • Do not miss classes. However, you are allowed to be absent from the class for two times, no questions asked. You might want to use the freebee wisely. docs.text: TSE 5002 Foundation of Quantitative Methods National Tsing Hua University Fall 2025 Instructor: Eric S. Lin Contact Information: Office: CTM 712, Email: slin@mx.nthu.edu.tw, Phone: 574-2729 Time and Location: Monday 9:00-noon, Center of Innovative Incubator 2F-A10 Office Hours: By appointment Course Webpage: Course materials will be available on the web through eeclass. Teaching Assistant: Raktisud You are lucky to have XXX to be your TA. Teaching Assistant Hours: TBA TA will hold the office hours and also be available for consultation on homework. Course Description: TSE 5002 introduces a range of quantitative tools that are commonly used to inform public policy issues. It provides an introduction to descriptive statistics, probability theory, statistical inference, and decision analysis. Our goal is that by the end of this course you will be able to: 1. Take a data set and a broad descriptive policy question (such as “What has happened to income distribution in Taiwan in the last 30 years?”), figure out what statistical analysis would be most appropriate to answer the question, conduct such an analysis, and present the findings in a way that is accessible to policymakers. 2. Identify real world policy situations in which the tools of probability can be used, identify which tools are most relevant, and critically consume policy analysis in which probability is used. 3. Critically consume policy studies/papers/reports in which statistical analysis is used. 4. Use the decision analysis framework as one tool to make personal and professional decisions, and to think about policy problems. Syllabus Fall 2024 The course content is divided into four broad units: (1) Descriptive Statistics, (2) Prob- ability, (3) Statistical Inference, and (4) Regression. Although the aim will remain on the underlying theory, students will be given several opportunities to gain “hand on” experience with real data set through homework assign- ments. I would encourage students to make use of my office hours (or TA’s office hours) during the semester and not wait until the day before the exam. If you are having difficulty with concepts early on, then it is likely that your difficulties will snowball and that there will be insufficient time to deal with your puzzles close to the exams. So please make use of my office hours to sort out difficulties as they arise. Prerequisites: High school algebra/Calculus preferred but not required Suggested Textbook: Basically, I will hand out my own lecture notes which are the summary of textbooks. You may find a similar textbook to the following:  Moore, David S., McCabe, George P., Craig, Bruce A., 2021, Introduction to the prac- tice of statistics (10th Edition), Macmillan Learning. Of course, there are lots of textbooks related to this course. If you have enough time, it would be also beneficial to check out some of the following reference books. References: Note that you don’t need to buy the following books. The book list is just for your reference.  Gujarati, D. N., 2003, Basic Econometrics, McGraw-Hill.  Wooldridge, J. M., 2003, Introductory Econometrics: A modern approach, South- Western. It is a very popular undergraduate level textbook adopted in US. This book gives a huge amount of empirical examples and illustrates econometric concepts intuitively.  Maddala, G. S., 2001, Introduction to Econometrics, 3rd edition, Wiley. This book is well written and in general is deeper than our textbook. You could also find some fancy topics in Maddala’s book such as bootstrap, Jackknife and GMM.  Kennedy, P. A., 1998, A guide to Econometrics, 4th edition, MIT Press. This book tries to verbally explain difficult econometric ideas and avoids heavy math. – 2 – Syllabus Fall 2024  Pindyck, R. S. and L. R. Rubinfeld, 1998, Econometric Models and Economic Forecasts, McGraw-Hill. Ths is my econometric textbook when I was a junior. It is quite easy to read.  Ramanathan R., 2002, Introductory Econometrics with Applications, 5th edition, South- Western. This book provides a number of practical applications. It is also self-contained. In Chapter 14, the author demonstrates the various steps involved in carrying out an empirical research project.  Johnston and DiNardo, 1997, Econometric Methods, 4th edition, McGraw-Hill. If you are sort of familiar with matrix algebra, it is a nice book to build up the foundation of econometrics. It also serves the bridge to compensate the gap between undergraduate and graduate level econometrics. Software: You are welcome to use any econometric packages such as STATA, R, or Python. Grading: Several problem sets will be passed out during the semester. Although there are benefits to be obtained from working in groups I would advise against students free-riding off other students. There will be two midterms and a final. Note that overdue assignment will NOT be accepted unless accompanied by a medical certificate. The same is true for the exams. docs.text: 1 TSE – Taipei School of Economics and Political Science Syllabus – 2024 FALL [Version May 25, 2024 / with dates to be updated] PERSPECTIVES IN INTERNATIONAL POLITICAL ECONOMY : (國際政治經濟) The Age of Disruption Instructor: Yves Tiberghien (Professor, Dept. of Political Science, UBC and Visiting Professor, TSE) Email: yves.tiberghien@ubc.ca Twitter: @Yves_Global Instructor Bio: https://politics.ubc.ca/persons/yves-tiberghien/ Course Schedule: TBC, lecture room A10 TBC Course Description: This course focuses on the foundations of international political economy, both theoretically and substantively. We initially discuss the various theoretical approaches to IPE, as well as key debates in trade, finance, currency, and investment questions. It also applies the theories and frameworks of IPE to the great questions of our time: the role of governance in markets, changing political economy of development, overcoming the resource curse, the transition of global economic order and hegemonic transition, climate political economy and the green technology revolution, digital and AI political economy, global sanction politics, and others. The session brings all frameworks down to the level of concrete empirical policy questions. Context: This course offers the tools and methods to understand the current remaking of the global economic order since 2008. The time for incremental changes within a stable structure is over. 2 The current battle is over the structure itself. Some pillars remain resilient, and are even expanding, owing to innovative entrepreneurship. But most are fragmenting, decaying, or being redrawn through shifting domestic forces and strategic competition. Will the postwar global order survive? And what explains the different trajectories of key regimes of globalization? We face an age of unprecedented global disruptions and systemic risks. Global governance constitutes one of the key challenges in current international relations and policy- making. As demonstrated by the Covid-19 pandemic, climate change, or the global financial crisis of 2008, global forces often overwhelm a political system that is primarily rooted in fragmented national sovereignty. As the global challenges facing the nations of the earth become more pressing, it becomes critical to address the classical political dilemmas of collective action, global commons, and asymmetry of benefits and costs. Are the dominant players in the system able to make progress in this large battle? The age of a stable US-dominated order is over. We have entered a period of great competition for global rules and norms, a battle between connectivity and fragmentation, and a confrontation between old powers and new rising powers. We are also facing a perfect storm that combines globalization-induced dislocations and a democratic crisis in US and Europe; a large-scale Russian war in Ukraine with ripple effects across the world; a climate change crisis challenging our entire economic model; the greatest pandemic since 1919; a powerful AI-centered/digital technological revolution; the greatest shift in the balance of power in over a century (over 20% of economic power shifting hands from advanced Western democracies to emerging countries between 2000 and 2018); the massive and threatening rise of China; and a US President bent on unraveling the economic and security institutions patiently built since 1944. Asia and soon Africa are rising across the board in all sub- regions, recovering a voice that was lost since pre-colonial times, ushering a much more diverse and multipolar world. According to the IMF’s current forecasts, over 60% of world economic growth will take place in Asia between now and 2030. The two dominant powers, the US and China, are locked into an ever-worsening spiral of trade conflict and security competition, a process made worse by misperceptions and emotional reactions and threatening to engulf the world economy. Is the US intent on destroying the rules-based order it nurtured for decades, in order to stop the rise of China? Or is the US just seeking to adjust rules and the division of benefits? Is China intent on uprooting the Western liberal order, or is China just seeking to gain a bigger voice within existing economic and global institutions, while retaining its historically- derived governance? The course will include a variety of activities, including lively lectures, guest speakers, movie excerpts, discussions, and debates. Invitations to global online events will be included. The instructor will be available for further discussion in person or by email. Key Words: Global trade, great transformation, disruptions, systemic crisis, technological change, global governance, Covid-19 Crisis, G20, global finance, Digital governance, AI, 5G, climate change, 3 rise of China, development (including AIIB), SDGs and Agenda 2030, global rules, globalization, global trade (TPP, RCEP) Learning Outcomes / Course Objectives 1. Understand the origins of the modern global economic system and its historic phases 2. Understand and be able to present arguments according to the various key theoretical models of IPE 3. Understand and be able to work with key debates regarding global trade, global finance, global currency, global investment, and global economic norms. 4. Understand the concept and pillars of the global economic order 5. Explain theoretical dilemmas of global governance in the current age; Unpack the process of creating global governance (comparing different arenas); Develop a pathway to analyze and solve governance problems; 6. Explain the particular historical juncture of our current period in a larger comparative perspective with a focus on the interplay between the US, the EU, Japan, and large emerging powers (China, India, Brazil) among others. 7. Provide a detailed overview, from the perspective of global governance and a changing balance of power, of five issue areas: global finance, development/SDGS, climate change, pandemic governance, and digital governance 8. In addition, students will be actively involved in the course through participation and debates and will thus improve their analytical and presentation skills. Professional Skills - Analytical and theoretical skills - Management: project management; team work - Communication: oral and written; multiculturalism, negotiation - Performance: research and analysis, critical thinking, creative thinking; and problem- solving - Entrepreneurial Spirit Assessment and Grade Distribution: Session Participation: 15% Session Presentation: 15% Short Paper (Summit Report) 20% October 23 Think Piece Paper (10-12 pages): 50%. [due Jan 20] Required readings (per syllabus) consist of selected book chapters and articles. These readings are available as PDF pieces. 4 The course will operate as a combination of both lively lectures (with text available on the website) complemented with occasional documentaries AND session discussion and debates. From the third or fourth session onward, each session will start with a student-led presentation on the topic and a first round of student-led discussion to unpack key issues in an interactive way. This discussion will be followed by a lecture and further discussion. Readings are important to complement the lectures and material covered in session. You are expected to finish the readings by the night before our session. Participation: Given the interactive nature of this course (half lecture, half discussion), I give a lot of importance to participation. I will moderate discussions to ensure that everyone has a chance to participate. Participation grades will be given both on quantity and quality of interventions (but mostly quality). I will encourage lively debates and confrontations of ideas. Session Presentation Participants will be divided into groups. Each group will be in charge of taking the lead for the seminar beginning session 3 or 4. The group will open the seminar with a 15-20mn (MAX) lively presentation exposing the key questions of the given week and reviewing key approaches and empirical results to answer these questions (based on the readings assigned for this week). Participants will then put 1 or 2 questions to the session and will moderate the ensuing 30-minute discussion. This first part will not exceed 55 mn in total (presentation+ discussion). A common grade will be assigned to the group members. Short Paper (5-7 pages, double-spaced): Summit Report You may join any global summit or significant workshop (mostly online, live or recorded) from a range of options related to global governance or global order: global online summits, global institutional summits, Paris Peace Forum, global think tank events, global NGO event, academic workshops. I will send you many invitations to global summits, but you are not limited to those. It should be a workshop that goes beyond a single talk by one speaker to hear a range of views. Your report will include the following elements: - 1. Introduction on scope, contribution and potential limits from the summit - 2. Summary of key takeaways from the summit, salient ideas, moments - 3. Analysis and Discussion in reference to some readings, theories, frameworks, and discussions of this course (ie a contextual analytical discussion). This could extract bigger trends and lessons in either decay, disruption, or resilience or innovation in the broad global governance system. - 4. Concluding part with your own voice covering either major implications or ideas for future research, or presenting your policy proposal to address issues discussed at this workshop and take them to a new dimension. 5 Think Piece Paper (10-12 pages, double-spaced): Think pieces have 2 major goals: first to develop a personal interpretation of IPE issues by presenting your own argument and defending it in a few pages; second, to demonstrate your mastery of the readings and facts presented in lectures. The questions are given by the instructor. (pick one from a choice of 5). Your paper should be an essay. Specifically, the paper must do the following three things: 1. Present an analytical argument that is a clear answer to the question 2. Address some of the literature related to the question (possible answers) 3. Offer some compelling evidence to support your argument (taken from readings, lectures, and session web links) ** Highly Recommended Regular Sources on Current Global Politics ** Good Global News Sources: - The Financial Times; New York Times, including The Daily podcast - OpenCanada.Org weekly news - Foreign Affairs; The Economist - Global Summitry Project Podcast, https://globalsummitryproject.com/podcasts/ Updated Think Tanks and Sources: - HIGHLY RECOMMENDED: *** CSIS. Economy Disrupted Series. 2020-2021. https://www.csis.org/programs/economics-program/economy-disrupted - *** Brookings International Affairs (and the US page as well) + related podcasts: https://www.brookings.edu/topic/international-affairs/ - *** Chad Bown and Peterson Institute of International Economics (including his weekly podcast on the Trade War) and twitter feed: https://piie.com/experts/senior-research- staff/chad-p-bown - Project Syndicate, a leading opinion page with many renowned scholars as columnists (such as Dani Rodrik and Barry Eichengreen): https://www.project-syndicate.org - Great podcast: Global Summitry Project Podcast (Chaired by Dr. Alan Alexandroff, U of Toronto) https://globalsummitryproject.com/podcasts/ - CSIS (Washington DC) and relevant podcasts (including tweets and papers by Scott Kennedy and Scott Johnson, China Power podcast, and Trade Guys podcast): https://www.csis.org/regions/asia/china Good Sources on China and China-US Relations (besides those cited above): - The China Project and Sinica Podcast: high quality updates and regular podcast, including review of Chinese sources: https://supchina.com - Regular Updates from Brookings Thornton China Center: https://www.brookings.edu/center/john-l-thornton-china-center/ - Bill Bishop’s Daily News (on Tweeter or subscribe) 6 - South China Morning Post (SCMP) 7 Course Outline and Readings Part I: Key Concepts and Debates Week 1 (9/13): Introduction of IPE today: Global Political Economic System under Stress Week 2 (9/20): Historical Perspective on the Global Economy Week 3 (9/27): Conceptual Building Blocks: Theories of IPE and their Limits Week 4 (10/4): Core Concepts: Collective Action, Institutions, Interests, Ideas Week 5 (10/11): Human Cognition, Interactions, and the Struggle with Global Cooperation Part II: Global Economic Order and Globalization Week 6 (10/18): Mapping out Disruptions and Systemic Risks Week 7 (10/25). Erosion & Innovation in Global Gov.: Fragmentation, Resilience, Entrepreneurship Week 8 (11/1): Globalization and social fragmentation: Causes and Political Impact Week 9 (11/8): Power transition – Power Shift and Securitization of global public goods Part III: Empirical Debates in the Current Age Week 10 (11/22): Global Trade Fragmentation: Competition and Domestic Contestation Week 11 (11/29): Financial Crises and G20 as Global Order Laboratory Week 12 (12/6): Digital Governance (Part 1): Data Regulation and Fragmentation of the Internet Week 13 (12/13): AI Governance Week 14 (12/20): The Global Political Economy of the Covid-19 Pandemic Week 15 (12/27): Climate Change, Green Technology Competition, the Transformation of IPE Week 16 (1/3): Escaping the Resource Curse 8 Week 17 (1/10): Toward a Paradigm Shift: Global Development Regime (SDGs) List of Presenters – TBD in the second session Weeks 3. These little computer 33 chips provide the processing power for everything from cars and iPhones, to unmanned drones and missiles. In Beijing's Made in China 2025 industrial strategy, through which China seeks to move up the value chain to become a high-tech superpower, semiconductor self-sufficiency was one of the targets. Beijing is falling far behind on this target. MIC 2025 stated the aim of meeting 70 per cent of China's demand through domestic production by 2025, but, seven years on, it is only meeting 20 per cent of its domestic needs (by one estimate). The world's leading manufacturer of semiconductors is in fact in Taiwan. The Taiwanese Semiconductor Manufacturing Company dominates more than half the global market, and controls 90 per cent of the cutting edge 5 to 10 nanometre sector (in this industry, size matters; the smaller the chip, the better). Even American companies like Intel outsource a substantial amount of production to TSMC. A tech arms race is underway. In order to control the supply of this small but vital component, China and the US are desperately funnelling money into their own national champions, whilst 'kneecapping' each other's efforts, as my guest Nigel Inkster tells me on this episode. He's the former director of operations and intelligence at MI6 and author of The Great Decoupling: China, America and the Struggle for Technological Supremacy . On Tuesday, GPT-4 was released, and its capabilities are stunning, and in some cases, chilling. More on that in Tuesday’s episode. But I wanted to take a moment to talk through my own views on A.I. and how I’ve arrived at them. I’ve come to believe that we’re in a potentially brief interregnum before the pace of change accelerates to a rate that is far faster than is safe for society. Here’s why. docs.text: 1 Civilizations, Empires and World Order Professor Amitav Acharya Introduction The 21st century is witnessing the end of the “great divergence” between the West and the Rest, which began with the rapid ascent of Western Europe from the 17th century AD onwards and the corresponding decline of the once mighty and wealthy civilizations, such as those of China, India, and Islam. As the global power and idea shifts reshape dynamics of world politics civilizational identities are asserting themselves, creating fears of what Samuel Huntington called a “clash of civilizations”. At the same time, the relative decline of the West, the crisis in the US- led liberal hegemonic order and the increasingly global role of rising powers such as China and India in world affairs are creating new possibilities of both conflict and mutual learning and cooperation between the West and the Rest. Against this backdrop, it has become ever more important to revisit the concepts of “civilization” and “world order”, to examine them from a historical and global perspective, to analyze their interaction and inter-relationships through the ages, and to draw lessons for the present and the future. Aside from its intellectual and analytical purpose, this course has a normative inspiration: to promote greater diversity and inclusion in international studies. According to its foundational narrative, the field of International Relations (IR) was “born” in the UK, and “raised” in the US; hence its labelling as an “American social science” (in Stanley Hoffmann’s phrase),. The conventional study of international relations relies heavily on concepts and practices developed in Europe and the US. This course (due to lack of time, it has a primary focus on China, India and Islam, but brings in others) challenges the Western-centric narrative of IR and opens the door to a Global International Relations (Global IR). While conventional IR uses the nation-state as the unit of analysis, the Global IR approach takes civilizations as the basis unit to explore the multiple types of international systems or world orders, including those that predate the Westphalian system and the rise of the West. If one approaches IR (or “world politics” or “international studies”) with the nation-state as its core unit of analysis, one has less than 400 years of history to play with. This is also the period of the rise and dominance of the West. If one studies IR and related fields from the perspective of civilizations, then one has over 4000 years of human history to reflect on and analyze. In this broad sweep of history, many civilizations have risen, fallen, and reemerged. No civilization can claim a monopoly over ideas or approaches to peace, security, diplomacy, development, human rights, environmental protection, or other related subject-matter of IR. By taking a broad historical perspective, this course aims to uncover the forgotten or marginalized agency of non- Western civilizations in the making of the modern world order, and stress the multiple, global origins of international relations and world politics. This “Global IR” approach not only helps us to better understand the contemporary dynamics of world politics, but also promotes inclusiveness in our increasingly complex, diverse and multicultural world. Learning Objectives 2 In completing this course, students should have developed: 1. Broad familiarity with the history of civilizations and world orders, especially the major civilizations such as China, India, Islam and their impact on the world orders of their times; 2. Ability to analyze the key factors behind the rise of the West and the role played by non- Western civilizations in contributing to it and recognize the historical and cultural forces that have shaped the contemporary world order and will shape the future; 3. Understand and appreciate the multiple foundations of theories and concepts of the discipline of International Relations (IR) and question the present state of IR as a Eurocentric or Western-centric field of study; 4. Enhanced critical thinking, including ability to interpret and present international affairs from multiple cultural and philosophical perspectives; 5. Understand and analyze the key forces shaping world politics today, including the role of emerging powers such as China and India, trends in global governance, conflict and cooperation among nations and states; 6. Sensitivity to, and respect for, diversity and inclusion in the study international affairs. Texts: 1. Henry Kissinger, World Order (New York: Penguin, 2014) 2. Amitav Acharya, The End of American World Order, 2nd edn. (Cambridge, Polity, 2018) Assignments: A. docs.text: Keywords: China, BRI, Global South, infrastructure, SEZs, extractive industries, environmental impact Course Title: China and the Global South TSE Fall Semester 2025-26 Draft 5-25 [some readings might be swapped out, as this is a field that is changing all the time] Julia C. Strauss Class time: Friday, 10-1 Lecture Room: Office: Office Hours： Fridays 1-2 pm and by appointment online E-mail: js11@soas.ac.uk Description As China is an increasingly important player in world politics, its profile as a non-traditional donor to other developing countries has risen. Yet there is a great deal of (mis)information and at best only partial understanding of its “rise” for the Global South. This weekly seminar seeks to overcome a range of (mis)perceptions about China and the Global South that are regularly (re)told and (re)presented in the open media and in think tanks outside China. After considering what is and is not different about China’s approaches to development and aid, we disaggregate “China” as comprising a multiplicity of actors who “go out” to the Global South in search of investment, aid, and employment in quite different sectors. Weeks 5-7 concentrate on what China makes available to the Global South in terms of infrastructure and investment; Weeks 8-9 turn to the sheer scale and local impacts what China’s rapid industrial growth has meant for primary commodities from the Global South. Weeks 10-11 address questions of China’s “soft power” and environmental impacts in the Global South. Throughout the class we will focus on the ways in which neither China nor countries in the Global South are unified: each is comprised of an ever shifting range of different political, social, and economic actors. After Week 12, we will shift to discussion and presentation of students’ final projects. Course Objectives For students to: 1) Develop greater understanding of the drivers behind China’s sets of relationships with the Global South 2) Develop critical awareness of the rhetoric and claims for and against China’s growing relationships with the Global South through the BRI 3) Hone critical ability to analyse particular instances of China’s projects in the Global South 4) Develop critical and writing skills in policy analysis through the writing of short policy briefs and a longer piece of policy analysis Course Delivery Until the last week in November, will be face to face, and we will meet weekly. Once we shift to “Flipped learning” in the last two weeks of the semester before the examination period, there will be no regularly scheduled class, but I will continue to be available for consultation remotely. Until Week Eleven, the normal format of the seminar will be that I will lecture for a bit more than an hour, followed by a short break, and the rest of the time will be given over to student presentation, discussion, and other exercises TBA. Weeks Eleven and Twelve will be devoted to student presentation of their final projects and discussion. Weeks Thirteen and Fourteen are “Flipped Learning” from then until the Monday of Exam Week, you should be working on your policy report/ final project. There will be no final exam. Course Requirements A) Reading Requirements All students will be expected to have done the reading for the weekly seminar an advance of the class meeting itself. I try to mix up longer, often more academic articles or book chapters with shorter policy or opinion pieces. But if you are to get much at all out of this class, then you need to come to class prepared, and this means having engaged with the reading and the topic before the seminar! B) While there are no specific textbooks for this class, and the topic is changing so rapidly that I will almost certainly have to swap out individual readings as new ones become available, there are several book length treatments of the topic that are especially noteworthy that I hope that the library will procure: 1. Min Ye, The Belt Road and Beyond: State-Mobilized Globalization in China: 1998–2018 (Cambridge University Press, 2020) 2. David Lampton, Selina Ho, and Cheng-chwee Kuik, Rivers of Iron: Railroads and Chinese Power in Southeast Asia (University of California Press 2022) 3. Miriam Driessen, Tales of Hope, Tastes of Bitterness: Chinese Road Builders in Ethiopia (Hong Kong University Press, 2019) 4. Axel Dreher, Adreas Fuchs et al, Banking on Beijing: The Aims and Impacts of China’s Overseas Development Program (Cambridge, 2022) 5. Austin Strange, Chinese Global Infrastructure (Cambridge Elements, 2024), https://www.cambridge.org/core/elements/chinese-global- infrastructure/35932BF8AEADDEFF1E96B19B13300FAE (free download) C) Writing Requirements 1. One short (500-750 words) critical response paper: due by the end of Tuesday 17 September(10 %) 2. One short (1,000- 1,250 word ) policy brief : due end of Week Eight before class on Friday 24 October (15%) 3. One abstract/ short bibliography for final essay/ policy report : not formally assessed but necessary to finalize your topics. DUE BEFORE the end of MONDAY 11 November . This will not be graded, but is important for feedback prior to your presentations. 4. One policy report OR regular analytical academic essay on a topic involving China and the Global South that covers some aspect of China’s investment/ aid/projects/ trade/ migration / environmental impact etc. You do not have to choose a topic that is explicitly covered in this class, but it should broadly align with the themes of the course and not be primarily focused on either military or security issues. (5,000-7,000 words), due BEFORE the beginning of regular exams on Monday 15 December 2024 (50%) D) Oral Requirements 1. One 20 minute oral + ppt presentation on your chosen topic for your final policy report/ paper, date TBA in either Week 11 or Week 12 (15%) 2. Regular participation and preparation in seminar discussions. (10%) This breaks down into two components: a. Taking on presentation of the seminar readings for the week and participating in other exercises b. Regular attendance in class (attendance will be taken from Week Three, and without a reasonable excuse, deductions will be made for non-attendance) c. Regular and meaningful participation and discussion even when you are not a presenter Statement on Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in this class Artificial Intelligence is an increasingly powerful, and also easily misused, tool that researchers and writers at any level now cannot afford to ignore. I encourage the critical use of AI in this class (it is very helpful for organizing thoughts, sifting through references and bibliography, and checking text. However, the uncritical and unrestricted use of AI can equally lead to very large problems (false or misleading information, “tilt” towards what is popular rather than what is well referenced and well argued, overreliance on what is current and trendy rather than what has depth and might be older). Think of AI as an autocompletion and sorting tool: it can help you sort and get through routine tasks quickly, but it cannot substitute for either your thinking or the parameters that you put in when you ask it to do something. Therefore, the critical use of AI in this class is not only permitted, but encouraged. However, I do require that you indicate exactly when and how you use AI in all your written work. Schedule of Class Sessions: PART I: The Background [History matters] Week One [Friday 5 September]: Introductions, explanations, and reading texts on China and the Global South Readings, charts, and background on China’s domestic politics and policy making: https://multimedia.scmp.com/widgets/china/cpc- primer/?fbclid=IwAR0wOmmNM8myoMAf4qSgslc08d3eKk6THMEnvBb- WcauiKt8kVpobAsul2c Meg Rithmire, “Going Out or Opting Out? Capital, Political Vulnerability, and the State in China’s Outward Investment”, Harvard Business School Working Paper 20-009, https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/20-009_664c9264-f0ee- 4e43-acbd-d5da9f08caf1.pdf David Lampton, Selina Ho, and Cheng-chwee Kuik, Rivers of Iron: Railroads and Chinese Power in Southeast Asia University of California Press, 2020, pp. ix-xv For reference: https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Chinese-Communist-Party-Government- Structure_fig2_228409863?fbclid=IwAR1XZJODNq4lhAbYXcrZLfA5Sb2IICVe5E 7n2_KlmgnfxP707Fo2rukr-2A https://www.cfr.org/backgrounder/chinese-communist- party?fbclid=IwAR3WMfeeXbFIUwVXsFWh1VOcTGqxE0gsDG9anaKOQhmXw uBdhb2tyIYrFrU Kenneth Lieberthal, Governing China: From Revolution Through Reform 2nd edition, Norton, pp. 3-26, 171-240. (introduction, and parts of chapters 6 and 7). The Lieberthal reading is old, but is still one of the better explanations of a political system that is often opaque. Recommended: Julia C. Strauss, “The Past in the Present: Historical and Rhetorical Lineages in China’s Relations with Africa”, The China Quarterly 199, September 2009, pp. 777– 795, doi:10.1017/S0305741009990208 PART I – The Grand Principles and Core Institutions Behind China’s Engagement with the Global South Week Two [Friday, 12 September] Ideals and Institutions: What is the Belt and Road Initiative [BRI], and how is it implemented? {aka “Follow the Money”} Readings: “Full text of President Xi's speech at opening of Belt and Road forum,” Xinhua, May 14, 2017 http://www.xinhuanet.com/english/2017-05/14/c_136282982.htm Min Ye, The Belt Road and Beyond: State-Mobilized Globalization in China: 1998–2018 (Cambridge University Press, 2020), pp. 26-49 Yuen Yuen Ang. “Demystifying China’s Belt and Road: The Struggle to Define China’s Project of the Century,” Foreign Affairs, May 22, 2019 https://www.foreignaffairs.com/articles/china/2019-05-22/demystifying-belt-and- road Brahma Chellaney. “China’s debt trap diplomacy.” Project Syndicate. Jan 23, 2017. https://www.project-syndicate.org/commentary/china-one-belt-one-road-loans- debt-by-brahma-chellaney-2017-01 John Hurley, Scott Morris, and Gailyn Portelance. “Examining the debt implications of the BRI from a policy perspective.” Center for Global Development. March 2018 . Recommended: US-China Economic and Security Review Commission. Hearing on “China’s BRI: Five Years Later,” Jan 25, 2018. US-China Economic and Security Review Commission. https://www.uscc.gov/hearings/chinas-belt-and-road-initiative-five- years-later Austin Strange, Chinese Global Infrastructure (Cambridge Elements, 2024), https://www.cambridge.org/core/elements/chinese-global- infrastructure/35932BF8AEADDEFF1E96B19B13300FAE (free download) Michal Himmer & Zdeněk Rod: “Chinese debt trap diplomacy: reality or myth?”, Journal of the Indian Ocean Region, (2023) _DOI: 10.1080/19480881.2023.2195280 The Brautigam reading, “Misdiagnosing the Chinese Infrastructure Push” (required for next week) is also useful. Lina Benabdallah, “Contesting the international order by integrating it: the case of China’s Belt and Road Initiative”, Third World Quarterly 40:1, pp. 92-108, DOI: 10.1080/01436597.2018.1529539 ASSIGNMENT 1: CRITICAL RESPONSE PAPER Due by the END OF TUESDAY 16 SEPTEMBER Moramudali and Panduwawala offer one version of China’s lending and “debt diplomacy” in Sri Lanka and Sarvananthan suggests quite another. Write a critical response paper of around 750 words in which you engage the following question: Is China engaged in “debt diplomacy” in Sri Lanka? In addition to the Moramundi/ Panduwawala and Sarvananthan, Chellaney, Himmer/Rod, and Brautigam are worth consulting. The Primary readings to consult for this exercise are below: Umesh Moramudali and Thilina Panduwawala “Evolution of Chinese Lending to Sri Lanka Since the mid-2000s – Separating Myth from Reality”, CARI Policy Brief No 22 November 2022 Available at SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4305736 And Muttukrishna Sarvananthan, “Chinese Lending to Sri Lanka: a Factual Cum 'Reality' Check: a Rejoinder to Umesh Moramudali and Thilina Panduwawala (February 26, 2023). Available at SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4369990 or http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4369990. This said, you’ll have to refer to the Chellany article, which is foundational, and it might be useful to consult Hurley et al, and Brautigam from next week. III – China’s Engagement with the Global South – Implementation and the Range of Reactions A. Infrastructure --- the “Giving” Week Three [Friday 19 September] Roads, Rail and Ports Lecture: the Players who give, the Players who build, and the Players who host Readings: Deborah Brautigam and Kevin Gallagher, “Bartering Globalization: China’s Commodity backed Finance in Africa and Latin America”, Global Policy 5:3, September 2014, pp. 346-352 OR Deborah Brautigam. “Misdiagnosing the Chinese infrastructure push.” The American Interest. April 4, 2019. https://www.the-american- interest.com/2019/04/04/misdiagnosing-the-chinese-infrastructure-push/ Lampton, Ho and Kuik, Rivers of Iron: Railroads and Chinese Power in Southeast Asia, pp. 1-14, and Chapter 4, pp. 84-116. If you have an especial interest in rail, the rest of the book is well worth reading. Week Five [Friday, 3 October ] Special Economic Zones, FDI and Industrialization in the “Global South” Readings: Deborah Brautigam and Xiaoyang Tang, “Going Global in Groups”: Structural Transformation and China’s Special Economic Zones Overseas”, World Development Vol. 63, pp. 78-91, 2014. docs.text: 1 Updated June 7, 2024 Fall Semester 2024 Government and Politics in Asia (a two-credit course) Instructor: Tun-jen Cheng (tjchen@wm.edu or tjcheng7@gmail.com) Class hours: 9-11 am Tuesday Taiwan time, Fall 2024 Office hours: 3-5pm Wednesday, Taiwan time, for the first 7 weeks; thereafter 7-9 pm Wednesday Taiwan time; by appointment, please email two preferred time slots to Allan and me two days in advance to schedule a half-an-hour meeting Description: In half a century Asia has emerged as the most vibrant economic region on earth. It is essential to understand political underpinnings and consequences of this region’s economic transformation. Covering East Asia, Southeast Asia, and South Asia, this course is structured thematically. Within each theme, however, we will focus on country specific cases that are either standing alone or in paired or multiple comparisons, thereby combining thematic analysis and country specificities. Part I provides a historical and contemporary overview of Asian politics, examining dynasty legacy, colonial rule, decolonization, and state- and nation-building. For Part II, this seminar addresses salient aspects of regime dynamics in the context of economic development which is the most important goal for a country upon gaining political independence. Topic issues for these five sessions include regime type and economic growth, drivers, processes, and problems of democratic transitions, as well as patterns of political evolution. For Part III, this seminar dwells on political institutions and processes in Asian democracies, covering constitutional forms of government, political parties, political participation, political polarization, and contentious politics. The final part is devoted to a few leading issues of governance in resilient authoritarian politics, including the implicit social contract, the political and economic conundrum, and intractable agency problems. Please note that the class and office hours will be in person during the first seven sessions; thereafter you continually come to our classroom while the instructor conducts the sessions remotely on GoogleMeet. Course requirements and grade distribution: 20% Attendance and participation 30% Midterm assignment (due 5pm Oct 21, 2024 Monday, Week VIII) 50% Term paper (due 5pm December 30, 2024 Monday, Week XVII) Reading materials for the course: All required readings are book chapters or journal articles. They will be available to you in softcopy. Note that a few book chapters are from the following three Routledge Handbooks: Tun-jen Cheng and Yun-han Chu, eds., Routledge Handbook of Democratization in East Asia, 2018; Paul Brass, ed. Routledge Handbook of South Asia Politics, 2012; Jeffrey Haynes, ed., Routledge Handbook of Democratization, 2010 [in which Southeast cases are predominant examples]. You are encouraged to but have no obligation to read any recommended readings. In addition, the instructor will inform you before each session which items in the required readings are for you to dive in, which other items are for you to skim over only. 2 Weekly Topics Part I. Pre-colonial Legacy, De-colonization, State-Building, and Nation-Building Sessions 1 & 2. Sept 3 & Sept 10 Course mechanics and an overview of Asian politics: patterns, distinct features, and puzzles;Pre-colonial and colonial legacies, decolonization, state-building and nation-building Required readings: Nayan Chanta, “When Asia was one,” Global Asia 2003, pp.58- 68; Chun-in Moon and Seung-won Suh, “Burden of the Past: history, identity, and nationalism in Northeast Asia,” Global Asia 2004, pp.34-48; Yuhua Wang, The Rise and Fall of Imperial China, Princeton University Press 2022, ch.1, pp.3-29. Recommended reading: Selections from Ebrey, Walthall, and Palais, East Asia, Houghton Mifflin 2009, pp.257-261, 296-303; Ian Talbot, “India and Pakistan: Colonialism, Nationalism, and Independence”; in Paul Brass ed., Routledge Handbook of South Asian Politics 2010, pp.27-41. Session 3. Sept 17 Mid-autumn holiday; no class; morning hours individual consultation hours (optional; by appointment) Part II Regime Dynamics and Economic Development Session 4. Sept 24 State capacity and economic development Required readings: Atul Kohli, State-Directed Development, Cambridge University Press, 2004, Ch 1 Introduction pp.1-26; Ch 2 The Colonial Origins of a Modern Political Economy: The Japanese Lineage of Korea’s Cohesive-Capitalist State, pp. 27-61, and Ch 6 “Origins of a Fragmented-Multiclass State and a Sluggish Economy: Colonial India,” pp.221-256. Recommended readings: Nicola Mastrorocco and Edoardo Teso, State Capacity as an Organizational Problem: the US experience, NBER August 21, 2023; Guo Xu, “The Cost of Patronage: Evidence from the British Empire,” American Economic Review 2018. Session 5. Oct 1 Regime type and economic change Required readings: Devin Joshi, “Multiparty Democracy and Economic Growth,” Taiwan Journal of Democracy, 2014, pp.25-46; John Harriss, “Political Change, Political Structure, and Indian State Since Independence,” in Brass, Routledge Handbook, pp.55-66; Stuart Corbridge, “The Political Economy of Development in India Since Independence,” in Brass, Routledge Handbook, pp305-320; Shahid Javed Burki, “Pakistan’s Politics and its Economy,” in Brass, Routledge Handbook, pp,83- 97; Stephen Haggard and Andrew MacIntyre, “The Political Economy of the Asian Economic Crisis,” Review of International Political Economy 5:3 (Autumn 1998), 381-392 Individual consultation hours on October 7 & 9 (by appointment) Session 6. Oct 8 Drivers and processes of democratic transition Required readings: Larry Diamond, The Spirit of Democracy, New York: Times Book 2009, ch 4 on the internal factors, pp.88-105, ch 5 on the external factors, pp.106-134, ch 6 on regional influence, pp.135-152, and ch 7 on what sustains democracy, pp.153- 3 168; Matthew Carlson, “East and Southeast Asia,” in Jeffrey Haynes, Routledge Handbook of Democratization, pp.129-144; Farida Jalazai, “Democracy in India and Pakistan: parallel past, divergent futures,” in Haynes, Routledge Handbook, pp.112- 128 Individual consultation hours on October 14 & 16 (by appointment) Session 7. Oct 15 Problems and challenges of new democracies Required readings: Thomas Carothers and Benjamin Press, “Understanding and Responding to Global Democratic Backsliding,” CEIP paper, 2022, pp.1-26; Tun-jen Cheng and Yun-han Chu, “An Overview of East Asian Democratization” and Yu- tzung Chang and Yun-han Chu, “East Asian Democratization in Comparative Perspective” both chapters in Cheng and Chu, Routledge Handbook of Democratization in East Asia, 2018, pp.1-17 and pp.19-39; Thomas Bruneau, “The Military,” in Haynes, Routledge Handbook, pp.207-221; Stephen Cohen, “The Militaries of South Asia,” in Brass, Routledge Handbook, pp,351-363 Midterm assignment due 5pm, October 21, Monday Session 8. Oct 22 Assessing India’s democracy under Modi: an in-depth case study Required readings: Sumit Ganguly, “Modi’s Undeclared Emergency,” Journal of Democracy, July 2023, pp.144-152; Maya Tudor, “Why India’s Democracy is Dying,” Journal of Democracy, July 2023, pp.121-132; Rahul Verma, “The Exaggerated Death of Indian Democracy,” Journal of Democracy, July 2023, pp.153- 161; Laura Gamboa, “How Oppositions Fight Back,” Journal of Democracy, July 2023, pp.90-104. Part III Democratic Institutions and Processes in Asia Session 9. Oct 29 Liberal democracy, electoral democracy and hybrid regime Required readings: Jorgen Moller, “The Gap between Electoral and Liberal Democracy Revisited,” Acta Politica, 42, 2007, pp.380-400; Gary Rodan and Kanishka Jayasuriya, “Hybrid Regimes,” in Haynes, Routledge Handbook of Democratization, pp.175-189; William Case, “Politics in Malaysia Today—Demise of the Hybrid? Not So Fast,” Taiwan Journal of Democracy December 2019, pp.1-30 and his “Regime Type and Pandemic Policy: Hybrid Exceptionalism in Malaysia,” Taiwan Journal of Democracy December 2020, pp.31-56. Session 10. Nov 5 Constitutional form of government Required readings: Juan Linz, “The Perils of Presidentialism” Journal of Democracy 1990, pp.51-69; Marco Bunte and Mark R. Thompson, “Perlous Presidentialism in Southeast Asia,” in Contemporary Politics, 2018, 42:3; pp.251-265; Jiunn-rong Yeh, “Constitutionalism and Judicial Review in East Asia,” in Cheng and Chu, Routledge Handbook, pp.225-248; Tun-jen Cheng, “Political Institutions and the Malaise of East Asian New Democracies,” Journal of East Asian Studies, 2003:3; pp.1-41. Session 11. Nov 12 Political parties and party system Required readings: Vicky Randall, “Political Parties,” in Haynes, Routledge Handbook, 2007, pp.222-236; Allen Hicken and Erik Martinez Kuhonta, “Introduction: Rethinking Party System Institutionalization in Asia,” in their eds., 4 Party System Institutionalization in Asia, Cambridge University Press 2015, pp.1-24 Session 12. Nov 19 Political participation Required readings: Zhengxu Wang and Leihua Ye, “Political Participation in East Asia,” in Cheng and Chu, Routledge Handbook, pp.251-268; Min-hua Huang, “Cognitive Involvement and Democratic Understanding,” in Cheng and Chu, Routledge Handbook 2018, pp.297-313; Pippa Norris, “Electoral Integrity in East Asia,” in Cheng and Chu, Routledge Handbook, pp. 405-424 Session 13. Nov 26 Political polarization Required readings: Krige Siebrits, Economc Inequality and Political Polarization,” Taiwan Journal of Democracy, July 2022, pp.41-60; Gordon Crawford and Abdul- Gafaru Abdulai, “Democratization, Poverty and Inequality,” in Haynes, Routledge Handbook, pp.353-367; Nae Young Lee and Sung Min Han, “Politics of Party Polarization in East Asia,” in Cheng and Chu, Routledge Handbook, pp.193-208; Thomas Carothers and Andrew O’Donohue, eds., Political Polarization in South and Southeast Asia: Old Divisions and New Dangers, CEIP 2020, pp.1-109 (read its brief introduction and one country chapter that interests you most). Session 14. Dec 3 Contentious politics Required readings: Meredith Weiss, “Resistance and Resilience: Copying With/Against the State,” Journal of Social Science Issues in Southeast Asia, 32:2; 2017; pp.374-404; Sumanta Banerjee, “Radical and Violent Political Movements,” in Brass, Routledge Handbook, pp.382-398; Stanley A Kochanek, “Corruption and the Criminalization of Politics in South Asia,” in Brass, Routledge Handbook, pp.364- 381; review Laura Gamboa, “How Oppositions Fight Back,” Journal of Democracy, July 2023, pp.90-104 Part IV Governance in Asian Authoritarian Regimes Session 15. Dec 10 An overview of resilient authoritarian systems in Asia; the grand bargain and the political and economic conundrum in China Required readings: Andrew Nathan, “Resilient Authoritarianism,” Bruce Gilley, “The Limits of Resilient Authoritarianism,” both in Journal of Democracy, 2003, pp.6-17, 18-27; Jessica Teets, Civil Society under Authoritarianism: the China Model, Cambridge University Press, 2014, ch.1, pp.38-78; Wei Shan and Yongnien Zheng, “Geopolitics and Democratization in East Asia,” in Cheng and Chu, Routledge Handbook, pp.509-527; Jeremy Wallace, Cities and Stability, Oxford University Press, 2014, ch.3, pp.43-70 ; skim through Dali Yang, “China’s Developmental Authoritarianism: Dynamics and Pitfalls,” in Cheng and Chu, Routledge Handbook, pp.122-141. Session 16. Dec 17 Intractable agency problems in China Required readings: Deborah Brown and Tun-jen Cheng, “The Vatican and the Chinese Party State: Where Do the Parallels End?” Orbis; Winter 2016, pp.72-86 Andrew Wedeman, “The Evolution of China’s Anti-Corruption Strategy,” in Cheng Chen and Meredith Weiss, eds., The Political Logics of Anticorruption Efforts in Asia, Albany: SUNY Press 2019, pp.201-228; Adam Posen, “The End of China’s Economic Miracle,” Foreign Affairs, August 2023, pp.1-8. 5 Midterm assignment: Pick a topic on political development or an essential aspect of political dimension of economic development in as many Asian nations as possible. Or you can pick two comparable cases. You can even do just one country. But no matter how many country cases you have, make good use of a database available in the field, and write a well-focused piece that is both theory informed and empirically substantiated. Term paper: You can pick a new topic or delve more in-depth into the topic that you have already dwelled on in your midterm paper. Consultation and mechanics of two writing projects: You are encouraged to come to my office for consultation for your topical choice. On both written assignments, you must provide appropriate citation for all thoughts, words, or ideas that are not your own (this includes the ideas of peers). An electronic file summarizing the Chicago Manual citation style will be posted on our class’ eeclass platform. The midterm assignment should be approximately 1500 words in length and the term paper approximately 3,000 words in length. Both should be submitted via email attachment in both Word and PDF formats. Both are to be turned in on time by 5 pm on the due date. Late submission triggers a loss of half a letter grade per day (that is, for an assignment turned in one day late and is an A quality one, the conferred grade will be A/A-; if it is turned in two days late, the conferred grade will be A-). AI policy: Using generative AI for this class is discouraged but not prohibited. Disclosure of its use is required. Expectations: • Class participation is a required part of the course. Please attend all classes and contribute towards discussion. • Writing, writing, writing: Learning to write well, to make a coherent and well researched argument, is one of the key skills you should get out of the grad school. • Current Events: A good theory, thesis, or analytical framework is a tool for digesting current events. Current events in turn allow us to assess the utility and limitation of the analytical tool. This is a very exciting time in Asian Politics with many daily changes in the region. I therefore strongly recommend that you follow current events in Asia by reading a major news source with good international coverage (i.e. BBC news, New York Times, The Economist etc.) or a news source from a subregion (i.e. Indian Express, Dawn, ToloNews etc.). This will help you get more out of the reading, by making class discussions more productive and improving the quality of your analytical thinking. docs.text: 1 Asian Development in Global Historical Perspective 歷史與全球觀點下的亞洲發展 Fall 2025 Instructor: R. Bin Wong, Distinguished Research Professor of History, UCLA Course Code TSE 602800 Place: Time: 10:10 AM – 1:00 PM Course Overview This course focuses on Asian economic development within a global context of industrialization & trade beginning in the late eighteenth century, moving through the 19th & 20th centuries, and looking forward into future 21st-c. possibilities. Central to this course are the economic and political principles and practices that together form the political economies of the past, present, and our possible futures. Each of the course’s four units devotes time to relationships between economic development and the natural environment in order to place our contemporary concerns about climate change in historical perspective and prepare future paths of economic and environmental change. Late 20th-century scientific research began to accumulate evidence confirming multiple ways in which the benefits of economic growth came at serious costs to the health of the natural environment and its plant and animal life. We therefore consider how the processes of modern industrialization that began less than 250 years ago depend on natural resources in ways unimaginable for most of the 300,000 years of human history. We begin in Unit I looking at Asian Development in the 19th-20th c. world of economic change and move in Unit II to placing Asian development within a global economic and environmental framework. The first half of the course brings us to the late 20th century and the recognition of limits to growth that leads us to Unit III where 21st-century efforts to foster sustainable development confront the challenges of achieving sustainability transformations. Unit IV concludes the course’s concern for understanding how economic activity depends on natural resources with a focus on energy development that is foundational to the economic security and wellbeing of people across Asia and the rest of the world. 2 Each of the four units considers relationships between economic development and the natural environment in order to place our contemporary concerns about climate change in historical perspective. Central to this course are the economic and political principles and practices that together form the political economies of the past, present, and possible futures we seek to create. This course aims to make your study of political economy prepare you to consider the type of 21st-century political economy you want to see emerge. Course Format 1. We meet in Weeks 1-5 and Weeks 7-12. Each three-hour session will include both lecture and discussion components. Weekly Study Guides with questions that highlight key themes to think about as you prepare the upcoming meeting’s readings will be posted to the class website at least a week in advance of the class meeting. Students are encouraged to take notes that summarize your understanding of the articles or portions of books that makes up each week’s readings. Having these notes will help you participate actively in each class as well as help you prepare the written work assigned in this course. Please be aware that you have readings to prepare before our first class meeting. 2. Readings for each class meeting can be found on our class website course syllabus links. 3. Please consider sending me an email by Tuesday evening regarding any questions you may have about any of week’s readings that I will try to address in my opening remarks. The more communication we have, the more effectively the course will succeed in teaching you ways to understand economic development. 4. Students will write and submit digitally three Response Essays that address one or more of the questions raised on the weekly study guides. The first Response Essay (1000 – 1500 words) will cover Units I & II and be due on October 9th (Week 6) at 1:00 pm. The second and third Response Essays (750-1250 words each) will cover Units III and IV respectively and be due on Saturdays (1:00 pm ) of Weeks 9 and 12. 5. These Response Essays along with the Study Guide notes you take on the weekly readings should prepare you for class lecture and discussion; they should also provide much of the basis for you to write your Final Papers. 6. Citations Format for the Response Essays and Final Paper should be made in a social science format of brief in-text citations (Author or Lead Author followed by “et al.”, then 3 publication date followed by page number(s)” and a bibliography organized by author or lead author’s last name followed by publication date and the title of book, book chapter or article; if you cite any PPT lecture material, in-text citation should be PPT title and slide number(s) and in the bibliography as “my name, week number, and PPT Title.” 7. The Final Paper assignment will be a 1,750-2,500-word double-spaced (7-10 pp) essay response to some selection of course themes. While I will offer you some themes for your final papers during Unit III, you can either select among the themes I suggest or propose your own theme. You’re encouraged to do some additional reading for your final paper. In past years, some students have incorporated materials regarding their home countries as part of the preparation of their final papers. Finally, I ask that you inform me by email the topic you choose for your final paper no later than Wednesday November 12th. Final papers are due Week 14 on Thursday December 11th by 5:00 pm TST. 8. Grading Please inform me if for any reason you will not be attending class as this is the norm typical in graduate school training (which a few students in the past did not realize). While there is no grading of class participation, there is an expectation of oral engagement with course material during class each week and if you’re not able to attend a class session, you’ll be expected to write some brief responses to the Study Guide Questions. Each Response Essay counts as 20% of your final course grade and the final paper 40% of your final course grade. The papers will have numerical grades converted to a final letter grade according to: A+ (97–100), A (93–96), A- (90–92), B+ (87–89), B (83–86), B- (80–82), C+ (77–79), C (73–76), C- (70–72), D+ (67–69), D (65–66), D- (below 65). To summarize, each paper gets a numerical grade with the sum of the numerical grades adding up to a potential maximum of 100 points. Ethics Statement on Generative Artificial Intelligence Grounded in the principles of transparency and responsibility, this course encourages students to leverage AI for developing their understanding of course materials. In accordance with the published Guidelines for Collaboration, Co-learning, and 4 Cultivation of Artificial Intelligence Competencies in University Education, this course adopts the following policy: Conditionally Open If you use generative AI in any of the four writing assignments, you must briefly explain how you used generative AI to develop your understanding of specific concepts, themes, arguments, and research methodologies in the readings. This explanation should be given below your paper title. If usage is discovered without proper disclosure, instructors, the institution, or relevant units have the right to reevaluate the assignment or report or withhold scores. I have not used generative AI to develop course materials or format. List of Unit Subjects, Session Themes, and the Readings I. Asian Development in the 19th-20th c. World of Economic Change A. docs.text: 1 Political Economy of the Semiconductor Industry Course Outline The semiconductor industry has become strategically important in economic growth and international relations. This course is designed to demystify the complexity of the global semiconductor industry in terms of technological development, market competition, geopolitics, and interactions of national policies. It is an interdisciplinary course bringing together the knowledge of engineering, management, economics, and political science. The course is divided into four parts and to be taught by four instructors, with each instructor covering a part of the course. The rest of the time will be used for examination and guest lectures. The four parts are (1) development of the semiconductor industry and technology, (2) characteristics and evolutions of the global semiconductor market, (3) geo-politics and geo-economics in the semiconductor industry, (4) technology policies pertinent to the semiconductor industry in East Asia. The detailed contents of each part are listed below. Topic II: How Taiwan developed its semiconductor industry (1975-1994). Topic III: Important technological breakthroughs in the semiconductor industry. Part 2 Global Semiconductor Market Description: This course is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the global semiconductor market and supply chains. Students will gain an in-depth understanding of the political and economic factors that drive the semiconductor industry, including market trends, supply chain dynamics, and the role of Taiwan in the industry. The course will cover key topics such as the semiconductor market by industry, by technology, and by region; the semiconductor supply chains; and 3 future challenges and opportunities in the semiconductor industry. Through lectures, case studies, discussions, and projects, students will develop a strong foundation in the political economy of the semiconductor industry and its role in global economics. Learning Outcomes: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to: • Understand the political and economic factors driving the global semiconductor market • Analyze trends in the semiconductor industry by industry, technology, and region • Understand the dynamics of the semiconductor supply chain • Assess the role of Taiwan in the semiconductor industry • Identify future challenges and opportunities in the semiconductor industry Course Topics: • Overview of the Global Semiconductor Industry • Market Trends by Industry, Technology, and Region • The Semiconductor Supply Chains • The Role of Taiwan in the Semiconductor Industry • Future Challenges and Opportunities in the Semiconductor Industry Recommended Reading: • Chris Miller, 2022, Chip War: The Fight for the World’s Most Critical Technology, London: Simon and Schuster. • Stephen Witt, 2025, The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, NVIDIA, and the World’s Most Coveted Microchip, Viking Book. docs.text: 1 COURSE SYLLABUS COURSE TITLE: International organizations in global politics Autumn 2025 • Credit: 2 • Time: T7T8 (Tuesday 15:30~16:20, 16:30~17:20) • Room: A10, TSE • Level: MA and PhD • Instructor : Gerald Chan, e-mail: cgcw@mx.nthu.edu.tw; gerald.chan@auckland.ac.nz • Office: C03, TSE • Office hour: Wednesday 13:00~15:00 or by appointment • Teaching assistant: TBC COURSE DESCRIPTION This course assesses the significance of international organizations in global politics. It focuses on the theoretical approaches to the study of international organizations, including the origins and development of these global bodies, especially the growth of regional organizations after the Second World War. The course explores the changing roles, functions and norms of these organizations working in such areas as security, economics, environment protection, human rights, public health, resource scarcity, science and technology, and social justice. How does the rise of Asian countries, in particular China, affect inter-state relations and the workings of international organizations? KEYWORDS International organizations, global issues, political economy, norms and rules, Asia, China LECTURE DATES & TOPICS Sep 2 Introduction Sep 9 Lecture 1 (L1): Globalization Sep 16 L2: Global governance Sep 23 L3: International organizations Sep 30 L4: Peace and security Oct 7 L5: Trade and finance Oct 14 L6: Environmental protection Oct 21 L7: Human rights Oct 28 L8: Humanitarian intervention Nov 4 L9: Public health 2 Nov 11 L10: Resource security Nov 18 L11: Poverty Nov 25 L12: Development Dec 2 L13: The digital world [Course instructor on conference leave] Dec 9 L14: Summary and conclusion Dec 16 Exam AIMS AND OBJECTIVES At the end of the course, we should be able to: 1. understand international relations and organisations in their many facets; 2. make a distinction between globalisation as a process and as an ideology; 3. examine the roles and functions of international organisations in conflict and cooperation; 4. assess the impact of the rise and fall of great powers on globalisation and global governance; and 5. probe a little into the future shape of globalisation. TEACHING METHOD Weekly lectures and/or tutorials/seminars where students make presentations for class discussion (to be arranged). docs.text: TSE 604900: Institutions and Economic Development Course Description The purpose of this course is to analyze institutions, and how institutions affect economic development. In addition to general analyses, institutions of China and China’s development are discussed with some details. The institutional component introduces analytical concepts and theoretical frameworks with historical and contemporary contexts. The economic component addresses economic development and political economic issues. It is a largely self-contained course on institutional economics, political economics, and Chinese political economy. Basic microeconomics and macroeconomics, development economics, political science, Chinese political economy are beneficial, but not as prerequisite knowledge. docs.text: 1 Trade and Regulations in the Digital Age Fall 2025 Professor Shin-yi PENG W6W7@TSE Overview This course examines international trade and regulations in the context of the digital economy. Newspaper headlines frequently highlight global trade challenges in the digital age, from disputes over semiconductor tariffs and national security-based 5G standards to data nationalism measures that restrict cross-border data flows. Governments are facing dilemmas between, on the one hand, maximizing opportunities stemming from the digital economy and, on the other, managing the associated risks and pursuing public policy objectives such as privacy and cybersecurity. The course begins by exploring regulatory frameworks for information and communication technology (ICT) products, with a particular focus on international trade rules and related disputes. It then turns to data-related domestic regulations, analyzing their impact on global trade and the balance among trade liberalization, industrial innovation, and digital sovereignty, particularly a nation’s right to regulate amid rising geopolitical tensions. Students will also study the role of international trade rules under the World Trade Organization (WTO), free trade agreements (FTAs), and digital economy agreements (DEAs) in shaping the digital economy. They will examine the interests of key stakeholders in international negotiations and identify areas where new trade rules and policies may be needed. Schedule (Provisional) Week 1 (9/3) Trade in Goods: Overview ICT Industrial Policy and Trade Rules Week 2 (9/10) Tariff War over Technology Export Controls on ICT Products Week 3 (9/17) Digital Economy and National Security Class Exercise: Moot Problem on ICT Trade Week 4 (9/24) International Standardization of ICT Products 2 Technical Barriers to Trade in ICT Products Week 5 (10/1) Trade in Services: Overview Digital Sovereignty and the Right to Regulate Week 6 (10/8) WTO Jurisprudence and Digital Trade Digital Services: Classification and Market Access Week 7 (10/15) Privacy, Cybersecurity and Global Trade Governance Week 8 (10/22) General and Security Exceptions to Digital Trade Rules Week 9 (10/29) No Class due to the University’s Annual Sports Day Week 10 (11/5) Data Nationalism and Data Localization Class Exercise: Multistakeholder Role-Playing Meeting on Data Localization Issues Week 11 (11/12) Digital Trade Rules in FTAs and DEAs Week 12 (11/19) Digital Platform and Trade Governance Week 13 (11/26) Artificial Intelligence and International Trade Law Week 14 (12/3) Digital Inclusion, Investment and Sustainability Class Exercise: Trade Negotiations Simulation Week 15 (12/10) Student Presentations Week 16 (12/17) Student Presentations Assessment Class participation (50%) Research paper (50%) A more detailed e-version of the syllabus, with reading materials and class exercises, will be provided in class.

docs.text: PERSPECTIVES IN COMPARATIVE POLITICAL ECONOMY Fall 2021 Chung-min Tsai <cmtsai@nccu.edu.tw> Time: TBA Location: TBA Office Hours: TBA This course provides a broad survey of some of the major debates in comparative political economy today, focusing especially on the creation, evolution and reform of market institutions. We begin by reading some of the classic works in political economy, including those of Smith, Marx, List, and Polanyi. We review some of the most influential works from four disciplines: History, Sociology, Economics, and Political Science. We then proceed with a selective survey of literature on the political economy of developed countries, newly industrialized economies, developing countries, and the post-Communist economies. The class concludes with the discussion on the post-globalization era and rise of state capitalism. COURSE REQUIREMENTS Response Papers (& a 15 page review essay for Ph.D. Students only) 60% Class participation 40% This is a reading and discussion seminar. Our class sessions will focus on discussions of course readings. All members of the seminar should complete the assigned readings prior to the seminar meeting and come prepared to discuss the readings - their relationship to one another, and their links to earlier readings and seminar discussions. Class discussion aims to achieve two goals: 1) identifying the key aspects of each work (i.e., main puzzle, major arguments, methodology, empirical evidence, etc.); 2) relating the different works to each other (i.e., comparison of focus or methodology, relevance to the development of the discipline, etc.). Every student has to make SOME substantive comments in each class session; I will call on students in case that should be required. Response papers: you will write TEN three-page response papers on the readings each week: 60% of total grade. These are due 11:59 P.M. on the Monday prior to each class and uploaded to the designated platform. NO LATE SUBMISSION. They should be no longer than 3 pages long, double-spaced, with 12-point, Times New Roman font. Response papers should address at least one of the following questions:  What are the principal differences in the arguments of the works under study?  What are the central debates in the field on the issue under consideration?  What are the main empirical strengths and weaknesses of the works under study?  Have the scholarly disputes/debates on this subject been resolved, and what remains to be discovered? 2 The paper should not be a mere summary of the readings but a critical commentary and a discussion of the issues that arise in the works. Good papers are the product of original thought and set forth a distinct hypothesis or interpretation of the relevant issues. Be focused, concise, and selective. They will be evaluated according to the effectiveness and insight with which they illuminate the principal debates and scholarly contributions to them in an independent and critically minded way. Review Essay (doctoral students only): Write a 12-15 page review essay on a specific topic according to the syllabus. There is no specific minimum or maximum number of books and/or articles to be covered in this assignment, but students should try to identify multiple perspectives and to review some of the best works on the topic.
