docs.text: Conflict and Peace Seung-hun Lee Fall 2025 Web: https://seunghunlee918.github.io E-mail: seunghunlee@mx.nthu.edu.tw TA: Su Mon Htet Naing TA mail: ekaterina.naing@gmail.com Class Hours: Fri. 9AM-12PM Office Hours: Thu. 3-5PM (Sign up here) Classroom: Innovative Incubation Hall A09 Office: Innovative Incubation Hall C06 1 Course Description Conflicts encompass a broad range of violent events that disrupt the economic and social stability of individuals and states, including crime, political violence, civil wars, and inter-state wars. Peace refers to the absence or resolution of conflict and the institutional and economic progress that helps prevent it. The existence of capable states that can prevent and mitigate conflict is crucial for peace. With the global rise in conflicts, it is essential to understand their origins and explore pathways to peace. This course covers topics in the political economy of development related to conflict and peace. The course will be organized around four key questions: What causes conflict? What are its consequences for individuals and states? How do individuals respond to conflicts? How can a state develop the capacities that allow it to maintain peace? Each class will consist of discussions on seminal papers, with two students taking turns presenting two selected papers. Throughout the semester, assignments will build the ability to critically engage with scholarly work, assess its claims, conduct empirical analysis, and develop original research that addresses gaps in the literature. 2 Prerequisites (MA students: Speak to me in person) • Familiarity with statistical inference: Students will assess empirical research and write a virtual paper demonstrating argumentation based on data. • (Not required, but helpful) Graduate-level micro/macroeconomics: Frameworks often in- volve game theory, constrained optimization, and principal-agent problems. 3 Lecture Materials and topics I will upload slides no later than the day before the lecture. Papers that will be discussed in the class will be presented in the latter half of this syllabus. There are no designated textbooks for 1 Conflict and Peace, Fall 2025 this course. However, the following books are recommended for understanding how economists and political scientists study conflicts and peace • Daron Acemoglu, James A. Robinson (2012), Why Nations Fail: The Origins of Power, Prosper- ity, and Poverty, Crown Business • Jean-Marie Baland, François Bourguignon, Jean-Phillipe Platteau, and Theirry Verdier (2020), Handbook of Economic Development and Institutions, Princeton University Press • Timothy Besley, and Torsten Persson (2011), Pillars of Prosperity: The Political Economics of Development Clusters, Princeton University Press • Chris Blattman (2022), Why We Fight: The Roots of War and the Paths to Peace, Viking The four topics covered in this course are as follows: 1. Cause of conflicts: Conflicts occur in many places, especially in developing countries. How do economic incentives drive individuals and states into conflict? How do political and ethnic dynamics lead to conflict? How and why do people engage in criminal activities? 2. Consequences of conflicts: Conflicts may undermine development prospects or trigger shifts that promote long-term progress. How do they affect the economic and non-economic out- comes of individuals? How do they shape economic development? How do they alter the institutional development of the state? 3. Response to conflicts: Individuals respond to conflicts by either fighting back or migrating. How do we overcome the collective action problems required to fight back? What causes people to migrate? What happens to migrants? How do people integrate to the host society after migration? 4. State capacity: An effective state can mobilize fiscal and human resources to prevent conflict and promote development. Why do some states fail at this? How do capable states build and maintain fiscal capacity? How do they manage personnel capacity? 4 Grading Policy Snap presentation (10%) Each week, two students will give a 15-minute presentation on two papers from the reading list (marked with double asterisks), with each student presenting one paper. The presenter will be chosen at random on the day of the class. Thus, everyone must prepare presentation slides for the two papers. Each presentation can use up to 8 slides (excluding title) covering: 1) moti- vation and research questions, 2) background, 3) data and empirical strategy, 4) key findings, 5) mechanisms, and 6) a critical self-assessment. This component evaluates students’ engagement with class materials and their ability to com- municate research clearly. Overly long or off-topic presentations are discouraged. 2/13 Conflict and Peace, Fall 2025 Replication exercise (20%) This exercise involves reproducing key findings from an empirical paper and submitting a report. Most empirical papers include data and code to allow others to verify the credibility of their results. Each student is expected to use R or Stata to replicate one of the following papers and check if the findings are reproduced by writing their own code. • Brodeur, Abel, (2018), “The Effect of Terrorism on Employment and Consumer Sentiment: Evidence from Successful and Failed Terror Attacks", American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 10(4), 246-282 • Campante, Felipe R, and Quoc-anh Do (2014), “Isolated Capital Cities, Accountability, and Corruption: Evidence from US States", American Economic Review, 104(8), 2456-2481 After completing the replication, each student should submit a report covering the following: • Are the data accessible? Some recent papers use administrative data, which are accurate but often restricted. Others construct datasets by merging publicly available sources. • Do the key findings replicate? Focus on replicating the most important tables or figures that support the paper’s core claims. Are your results similar or different? If different, how so? You must also submit your code (R or Stata) to demonstrate your independent effort. • Make your own extensions: Try alternative regression specifications, different choices of independent variables, sample restrictions, or falsification tests. You can use the original dataset or combine it with other sources. If extensions are not feasible due to data limita- tions, outline a detailed plan for how you would conduct the research differently. Final Exam (20%) There will be a cumulative exam focusing on the papers discussed in class, specifically those marked with single or double asterisks in the reading list. The questions will assess your un- derstanding of the theoretical frameworks covered and ask you to connect an empirical find- ing—either provided in the exam or drawn from the reading list—to a relevant theory. Virtual Paper (50%) Your assignment is to develop a viable paper plan that clearly motivates the research question, explains the background, data, and empirical strategy, and includes some preliminary results. The paper does not need to be complete—a half-finished but original and exciting project is preferred over a complete yet uninteresting one. The draft counts for 30% of your grade. You’ll deliver a 30-minute presentation of your virtual paper in the final class, which counts for 10%. The paper should be written in a scholarly article format. For instance: 1. Introduction: What is your research question? Why is it important from a scholarly or policy standpoint? 2. Literature review: What is the gap in the relevant literature? How are you filling that gap? 3/13 Conflict and Peace, Fall 2025 3. Background: What is the relevant information on the context that you are studying? 4. Data: What data source are you using or planning to use? Why should it be that dataset? 5. Empirical strategy: What statistical methods do you use? How do they allow for causal inference? What are the potential threats to that inference? 6. Preliminary results: What are the statistical relationships that you have found so far? 7. Mechanism and falsification tests: What factors may explain your main results? What are your plans to address potential factors that may nullify your findings? You will regularly discuss your virtual paper ideas with me. Four weeks before the vir- tual paper deadline, submit a 2-page research proposal outlining your question, contribution, background, and potential data sources. There is no need for results or detailed explanations on empirical strategy and falsification tests at this stage. This proposal counts for 10% of your grade. 5 Course Structure and Logistics Rules regarding collaboration Collaboration is encouraged assuming that (1) each student writes their own assignments, and (2) students must clearly identify their collaborators. Rules regarding AI usage AI tools may be used for assistive purposes only—such as proofreading, grammar checking, and coding support. However, using AI to generate complete assignments - presentations and take-home exams, in particular - is strictly prohibited. All submitted work, especially the virtual paper, must be original writing and analysis. One way to show that you are writing a paper with your own idea is to discuss your ideas with me throughout the office hours openly (without aid of AI). Any use of AI must be properly disclosed to the instructor. Violations will be treated as academic dishonesty and subject to disciplinary action under university policies. 6 Schedule and reading list The schedule is tentative and may change. Students are expected to prepare presentations on papers marked with double asterisks. Papers with a single asterisk will be discussed in class. Important deadlines • Presentation on research proposal: October 24th (Submit 2-page draft by email before class) • Replication exercise due date: November 21st, midnight (Submit codes and report by email) • Presentation on the virtual paper: December 5th, in class • Virtual Paper due date: December 21st, midnight (Submit the draft by email) • Final Exam: Week of December 19th, (exact time TBA) 4/13 Conflict and Peace, Fall 2025 6.1 Course Introduction and empirical analysis: Week 1 I will go over course organization, how to do assignments, and introduce the topics covered in this class. We will also discuss empirical frameworks necessary to understand the papers covered in this class. There will also be demonstration using Stata and R • Conceptualizing Treatment Effects • Ordinary least squares and randomized control trials • Panel regression • Instrumental variable methods • Difference-in-differences, event studies, and regression discontinuity 6.2 What causes conflicts: Week 2-4 Economic incentives behind conflicts • ** Berman, Eli, Michael Callen, Joseph H. docs.text: 1 Taipei School of Economics and Political Science (Fall, 2025) 11421TSED702300 Quantitative Methods II (數量方法二) Instructor: Min-Hua Huang (黃旻華) Class Time: Mon 13:20-16:20 Office Hours: By appointment Location: A09 classroom Email: mhhuang5103@ntu.edu.tw Course Description This course aims to train students with statistical skills to conduct multivariate regression analysis, including linear regression, ordinal logistic regression, multinomial logistic regression, and other advanced regression methods, such as multilevel modeling, panel regression, and psychometrics. The purpose is to equip student with proper capability to proceed causal investigation and able to do empirical research independently. This course will also introduce several large-scale public opinion datasets, including Asian Barometer, Arab Barometer, Afrobarometer, Latino Barometer, and Euraisa Barometer, and many others. Those datasets offer a rich source of information for students to engage in substantial studies in many subfields of political science. Background knowledge and theories that associated with those topics will be also covered in this course. Overall, the training of this course is not restricted to statistical methods, but also cover the realms of data collection and empirical analysis. Course Objective/Requirement This course proceeds with lectures and practical exercises. The topics cover basic mathematical skills (matrix algebra, calculus), probability theory, statistical estimation, regression analysis, hypothesis testing, statistical diagnosis, etc. There are two basic requirements: (1) complete weekly exercises on time; (2) participate in the final exams. Weekly topics will demonstrate how survey questions associate with theoretical concepts and apply to empirical research that results in journal publication. Grading Attendance and Discussion (10%), Weekly Assignments (40%), Midterm (20%), Final Exam (30%). AI Policy This course does not involve the use of AI.
